newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries start big week with soft bias.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries start big week with soft bias.

text.p: U.S. government debt markets started on a soft footing Monday before May personal income and consumption data, which kick off a holiday-shortened week crammed with important economic events.

"We have so much that's going to happen this week, so you have a little bit of a downward bias as we start the week," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany. "That is largely because last week we gave up about 12 basis points on long Treasuries."
Forecasters see income and spending, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, up 0.4 percent and 0.3 percent, respectively.
The long bond opened down 2/32 at 98-13/32 with a yield of 6.75 percent. The 10-year note was off 1/32 at 101-06/32, yielding 6.46 percent.
At 1000 EDT/1400 GMT comes May new home sales, which are expected by economists polled by Reuters to have increased to an annual rate of 786,000 from 772,000 in April.
But all eyes are on the first peek at important data for June -- the June index from the National Association of Purchasing Management on Tuesday, and the unemployment report on Thursday.
Analysts said a decision by the Federal Open Market Committee, which meets Tuesday and Wednesday, to hold interest rates steady is a foregone conclusion.

"The Fed meeting is pretty much a nothing because no one expects a rate hike out of them," said Doug Burtnick, senior fixed-income analyst at Technical Data. "The key points are the NAMP report tomorrow and the employment report on Thursday."
The June NAMP index, a key barometer of business conditions, is forecast to be 56.4, below May's 57.1 reading, but still well above the threshold showing expansion.

The June non-farm payrolls number, released one day early because markets will be closed Friday in observance of the U.S. Fourth of July holiday, is expected to be 222,000 after May's 138,000 increase.
Economists forecast the unemployment rate unchanged at 4.8 percent.
"Unless all of the data line up in a row being constructive for the market, we expect a range-driven week with a couple of bouts of volatility around the numbers," Burtnick said.
In other trade, the five-year note was off 2/32 at 99-18/32 to yield 6.35 percent.
At the short end of the maturity curve, the three-month bill was up two basis points at 5.02 percent and the six-month bill was up a basis point at 5.04 percent.
